messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir had been a paramedic for fifteen years, a man who believed he could function in the eye of any storm. That belief shattered six months ago on a rain-slicked stretch of the I-5. He was off-duty, driving home, when he came upon the multi-car pile-up. The flash of blue and red lights was as familiar to him as his own heartbeat, but the sight of his wife’s crumpled sedan pushed all the air from his lungs. His eight-year-old son, Omar, had been in the passenger seat. The moments that followed are a slideshow of sensory fragments for him now. He remembers the specific, sickening angle of Omar’s leg, the sight of the wound stark against his small frame. He remembers the smell, a nauseating mix of rain, gasoline, and the sterile, antiseptic odor from the first-aid kit he always kept in his car. But there are parts he cannot access, a black hole of several minutes between seeing the wreck and working on his own son in the back of the responding ambulance. No matter how hard he tries to retrieve that time, it remains blank, and trying to fill it brings on a wave of the same raw terror he felt then, a feeling of absolute, helpless freefall.

In the weeks after Omar was discharged from the hospital, a new, suffocating reality began to set in for Amir. He had come to believe that the man he was before the accident was gone forever, replaced by this hollowed-out, hyper-alert stranger. He saw himself as permanently damaged goods. At home, he found himself unable to sit still, throwing himself into tasks with a frantic energy—reorganizing the garage, fixing a fence that wasn’t broken—anything to occupy the space in his head where the memories threatened to bloom. When a memory did break through, it wasn't a simple recollection; it was a full-body hijacking. The faint smell of bleach his wife, Layla, used to clean the bathroom would suddenly become the overwhelming chemical sting of the ER, and he would be back in the ambulance, the phantom weight of his son's small body in his arms, the sirens screaming in his ears as if it were happening all over again.

His identity as a protector, both at home and at work, felt like a cruel joke. He was certain he had failed Omar in the most fundamental way, that a better father, a better paramedic, would have done something different. This conviction that he couldn't rely on himself began to seep into his professional life. He started calling in sick, avoiding shifts because the thought of the ambulance, the injuries, the very smell of the hospital, was unbearable. On the days he did force himself to go in, he was a ghost of his former self. He found his concentration shattered, unable to follow a simple briefing, his mind drifting back to the slick asphalt and broken glass. He would position himself in the station’s break room with his back to a corner, needing to see every entrance, a habit that drew quiet, concerned looks from his colleagues. The final straw at work was when a partner clapped him on the shoulder from behind to get his attention, and Amir flinched so violently he knocked a tray of supplies to the floor.

The tension followed him home. Layla’s gentle touch, once a comfort, now made him jump with alarm. The distance between them grew into a silent, painful chasm. It was after a particularly bad night, when he woke up shouting from a dream he couldn't remember, that Layla sat with him at the kitchen table and told him, her voice soft with worry, "I miss my husband. Omar misses his father. We need you back." Amir is now seeking help not because he believes he can be fixed—he is fairly certain that is impossible—but because the man he has become is a stranger to his own family. He is terrified that this broken version of himself is all that is left, but a small, desperate part of him hopes to one day be able to sit beside his son without seeing the ghost of his injuries, and to feel his wife’s touch as an act of love, not a threat.
